facts.fact_text: During the period 1990-97 Ilinden each year tried to organise meetings at sites in Pirin Macedonia to commemorate certain historical events.
On 18 April 1998 a number of members and followers of Ilinden from towns and villages in Pirin Macedonia tried to approach the Rozhen monastery by cars and by buses.
On 18 April 1998 all members and followers of Ilinden trying to approach the Rozhen monastery were turned back by the police who were placed at checkpoints on the roads leading to the monastery.
On 12 September 1998 members and followers of Ilinden tried to approach the memorial of Gotze Delchev in Blagoevgrad, but the police blocked their way.
On 25 April 1999 the police, who had dispatched patrols at all roads leading to the Rozhen monastery, blocked the way of members and followers of Ilinden and turned them back.

On 22 April 2000 members and followers of Ilinden who reached the Rozhen monastery site laid flowers and made a short speech, apparently denouncing the 'assimilation policy' led by the Bulgarian Government, after which they left the site.

On 18 April 1998 the passengers of one bus travelling to the Rozhen monastery were forced off and the driver was fined for allegedly driving a vehicle in a state of disrepair.

On 18 April 1998 one person coming by car to the Rozhen monastery was apparently taken into custody by the Sandanski police for ten hours for allegedly failing to produce an identification document, and was ill-treated.
On 12 September 1998 members and followers of Ilinden tried to approach the memorial of Gotze Delchev in Blagoevgrad, but the police blocked their way.
On 25 April 1999 the police, who had dispatched patrols at all roads leading to the Rozhen monastery, blocked the way of members and followers of Ilinden and turned them back.
On 25 April 1999 some drivers travelling to the Rozhen monastery were fined, allegedly for driving vehicles in a state of disrepair.

On 25 April 1999, on the way back from the Rozhen monastery, members of the Sandanski chapter of Ilinden tried to lay flowers at the bust of Yane Sandanski, but the police seized the flowers and allegedly arrested one person.
The applicants alleged that on 22 April 2000 a plain-clothes police officer was filming the participants at the Rozhen monastery despite their objections.

The applicants averred that on 22 April 2001 two members of Ilinden tried to place a wreath covered with a band with an inscription on the grave of Yane Sandanski, and that four policemen moved towards them and ordered that the band be removed.

The applicants averred that on 22 April 2001, when the persons carrying the wreath refused to remove the band, the police seized the wreath and arrested one of them, taking him to a nearby village, releasing him and warning him not to try to return to the meeting.
The applicants alleged that on 22 April 2001 a poster brought by members of Ilinden to the Rozhen monastery was taken away by a plainclothes police officer.
The applicants alleged that on 22 April 2001 the police prevented the placing on the podium of loudspeakers that members of Ilinden had brought to the Rozhen monastery.
The applicants alleged that on 22 April 2001 local catering companies were prohibited by the municipal authorities from sending staff and facilities to the Rozhen monastery site during the meeting.

On 12 September 2002 the police were present at the memorial of Gotze Delchev in Blagoevgrad and had formed a cordon between the members and followers of Ilinden and the hostile group, but apparently failed to prevent the above incidents.

Section 12(2) of the Meetings and Marches Act of 1990 provides that the President of the Executive Committee of the People's Council or the mayor shall be competent to prohibit the holding of a meeting, rally or march where reliable information exists that it aims at the violent overturning of constitutional public order or is directed against the territorial integrity of the country, would endanger public order in the local community, or would breach the rights and freedoms of others.
Section 12(3) of the Meetings and Marches Act of 1990 provides that the prohibition shall be imposed by a written reasoned act not later than twenty-four hours after the notification.
On 12 September 1998 members and followers of Ilinden tried to approach the memorial of Gotze Delchev in Blagoevgrad, but the police blocked their way.

On 12 September 1998 the police informed members and followers of Ilinden that the Blagoevgrad Regional Prosecutor's Office had banned the event and read them the decree, but refused to give them a copy.
On 4 May 1999 the police read out the Blagoevgrad Regional Prosecutor's Office decree prohibiting the event to members and followers of Ilinden, but refused to give them a copy.

On 12 September 2003 several police officers approached the members and followers of Ilinden in the centre of Blagoevgrad and read out a decree of the Blagoevgrad Regional Prosecutor's Office prohibiting the commemoration.

Section 12(3) of the Meetings and Marches Act of 1990 provides that the prohibition shall be imposed by a written reasoned act not later than twenty-four hours after the notification.
The Blagoevgrad Regional Prosecutor's Office decree of 17 April 1998 stated that the holding of the meeting by Ilinden would constitute an offence under Article 174a of the Criminal Code.

The Blagoevgrad Regional Prosecutor's Office decree of 28 July 1998 reasoned that Ilinden was not registered and hence had no right to organisational or political activities, and that the holding of a meeting would therefore constitute an offence under Article 174a of the Criminal Code.

The Blagoevgrad Regional Prosecutor's Office decree of 28 July 1998 reasoned that Ilinden was advocating changes in the constitutional order in Bulgaria and that the holding of a meeting would therefore also constitute an offence under Chapter 1 of the Criminal Code.
The Blagoevgrad Regional Prosecutor's Office decree of 11 September 1998 reasoned that Ilinden was not registered and hence had no right to organisational or political activities.
The Blagoevgrad Regional Prosecutor's Office decree of 11 September 1998 reasoned that Ilinden was advocating changes in the constitutional order of Bulgaria and expressed anti-Bulgarian views.
On 30 July 2000 certain members and followers of Ilinden were able to hold a meeting at Samuilova krepost, and it appears that the police did not interfere.

The Sofia Military Prosecutor's Office carried out a preliminary verification in response to Ilinden's complaint of 15 October 2002 and on 10 December 2002 refused to open criminal proceedings.

On appeal by Ilinden, the Sofia Military Prosecutor's Office decree of 10 December 2002 refusing to open criminal proceedings was upheld by the Sofia Military Appellate Prosecutor's Office on 20 February 2003.

Ilinden further appealed to the Chief Prosecutor's Office, which upheld the refusal to open criminal proceedings in a decree of 6 October 2003, reasoning that Ilinden's allegations were not supported by the facts established during the preliminary verification.
